new_statements.quote: In the notation primary stress is indicated by the acute accent (´) and secondary stress by the grave accent (`). Primary stress is accompanied by the highest tone of the word. The symbol r represents an alveolar flap.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Rendered PDF p. 1 (printed p. 113) of at 150 dpi and read the page image. The second introductory paragraph reads exactly: "In the notation primary stress is indicated by the acute accent (') and secondary stress by the grave accent (`). Primary stress is accompanied by the highest tone of the word. The symbol r represents an alveolar flap." (r underlined in print). Verbatim match; the. renders the two accent glyphs as (*) and (‘) but the image is unambiguous. The passage is preceded by the recording note (31 October 1973, elicited via Kâte, Sogum the consultant, "high degree of accuracy") and followed by the Pihom/Rai Coast classification paragraph, as the reader describes. No place…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The source states that Wasembo has primary and secondary word stress and that the primary-stressed syllable carries the word's highest pitch, but it gives no placement rule; stress is simply marked on every entry. Reading the marked forms on pp. 114-115 (from the page images): disyllables are mostly initial (kʰúha 'all', mása 'bad', mónu 'bird', kíma 'blunt', gúnu 'dam', máha 'dust') but bound verb/noun roots often end-stressed (hipá- 'anus', ekʰá- 'to dance', umé- 'to die', ipó- 'father', hoká- 'to cut'); trisyllables split between initial (námbehe 'banana', yóhoma 'bird of paradise', nínira 'black', hépera 'borer', námbiŋgi 'cassowary', mísiku 'childless', úteme 'fireplace', kákumu 'dust', wámbora 'floor') and second-syllable (kʰarána 'adze', itéme 'ashes', itépa 'bandicoot', awéhe 'blossom', naŋgóra 'cabbage', gobóre 'cloud', pukʰáne 'breadfruit', kiŋgáye 'blue', hoŋgáhi 'firefly', goráane 'egg'); so primary stress falls on the first or second syllable with no rule stated and no obvious segmental conditioning, hence the provisional 'lexical' reading. An alternative hypothesis the data would allow is weight-sensitivity (stressed long vowels in goráane, yaŋgáapu, akáaka), untested.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Marked with the grave accent. In four-syllable words it falls two syllables after an initial primary: émekàra 'between', úmbugùra 'cold', háwiràyo 'centipede', hónoŋgàri 'earthworm', mámaŋgàri 'fly', húŋgumugì- 'armpit', kúŋguŋgè- 'to dry'; also on a final root syllable after initial primary in pókʰonà- 'back', gébanè- 'chest', mágagè- 'chin', wákʰupʰè- 'blood'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; variant pairs such as omá-/óma- 'arm' and yóhɔ/yóho/uráho 'fire' show alternative stressings for the same gloss.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms in an elicited English-Wasembo wordlist (recorded 31 Oct 1973 through Kâte as the contact language, 'high degree of accuracy' claimed by the authors); nouns given with possessive-suffix hyphen and verbs as bound roots with hyphen, so the stress marks are on stems, not full inflected words. 'Highest tone of the word' means the stressed syllable carries the pitch peak; no tonal contrast is claimed.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1976 vocabulary and the 1975 sketch both name the language Wasembo (or Gusap), spoken in the five villages Gusap, Hinggia, Yankowan, Rampa and Maraboi east of the Gusap aerodrome, Markham headwaters, Morobe Province: this is wase1252 (Glottolog alternative names Gusap, Yankowan, Biapim). Jones 2023 calls the same language Horokoi (hh.bib: 'Horokoi = Wasembo [gsp]'). The wordlist data come from a single speaker, Sigkepe Sogum, village not stated.

sources.note: p. 113 introductory note: primary stress marked with acute, secondary with grave; primary stress carries the highest tone of the word; no placement rule given, but every entry in the 300-odd-word list is stress-marked (primary on 1st or 2nd syllable). SIL direct download is Cloudflare-blocked (403); copy taken from the Wayback Machine snapshot of 2024-07-31; image-only PDF, scanned at 300 dpi and the page images read directly for the accent marks.
Lists only Jones 2023, Claassen & McElhanon 1970 (p. 49) and Ethnologue; alternative names Biapim, Gusap, Wasembo, Yankowan; family Raic (Madang).
No phonology section; links the SIL vocabulary PDF and the Rosetta Project Swadesh list; cites Usher for classification closest to Yaganon.
